## Answer: 5,353,300

This is a derived result, not a recalled one. I verified the formula by hand for n = 1, 2, 3. For n = 200 it rests on extrapolating that pattern, not on a general proof.

**Reformulation.** A car at cell p facing direction d makes exactly one move per cell of its ray (the cells from p to the edge in direction d), plus the final exit move. So the total number of moves is n² + Σ|ray(p)|.

Reversing time turns removals into placements. Cars enter from the boundary and slide inward, and a car can only pass through cells that are still empty. So a configuration is removable exactly when there is an order on the cells in which each cell is placed before every cell in its ray.

**Reduced problem.** Build the grid one cell at a time. A cell may use direction d only if its whole ray is already built, and it then earns the ray length. Maximise the total reward.

**Construction.** Build rows from the bottom up, and within each row from right to left. Cell (r, c) can then take the longer of its upward ray (length r−1) or its rightward ray (length n−c). The reward sum is

Σ_{a,b=0}^{n−1} max(a, b) = n(n−1)(4n+1)/6.

**Small cases.** Let f(n) be the maximum total moves.
- n = 1: f = 1.
- n = 2: f = 7. A pinwheel of four outward-looking cars deadlocks, and the best feasible configuration gives 7.
- n = 3: f = 22. An upper bound from the rewards (corners can earn at most 6 in total, opposite edge pairs at most 3 per pair, centre at most 1) gives 13 for the reward sum, and a matching construction exists.

All three agree with the closed form

f(n) = n² + n(n−1)(4n+1)/6 = n(n+1)(4n−1)/6.

**Evaluate at n = 200.**

200 · 201 · 799 / 6 = 5,353,300

ANSWER: 5353300
